turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): He's four, bit wriggly and over it. Temp's 36.8, pulse a hundred and four. Weight 16.2 kilos.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks. Come through, grab a seat. What's been happening with him?
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's these dry patches. Behind his knees and in the elbows. Really itchy, he won't leave them alone.
[SEG0004] person_4 (PATIENT): Itchy. Stop.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): I know, mate, we'll go gentle. How long have the patches been there?
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Umm. About three weeks. And at night it's worse, he just...
[SEG0007] person_4 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): ...scratches till the sheet's a mess. We're up half the night and he's exhausted and cranky all day.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever with this?
[SEG0010] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. He's not been hot.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): What are you using on the skin?
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Err. Creams, mostly by the colour. Pink tube, a white one, and the big blue tub from the chemist.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you know the names, or what the label says?
[SEG0014] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The pink one says hydrocortazone, one percent. That's the steroid. We put that on twice a day. Mm, I suppose.
[SEG0015] person_1 (NURSE): Of. Blue tub in the bag is QV cream.
[SEG0016] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Right. Yeah, QV. Most nights we get the steroid on. Mornings we forget, sometimes.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any weeping, or yellow crust on the patches?
[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Umm. Sometimes, not really.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to creams or medicines?
[SEG0020] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anyone in the family with asthma or eczema?
[SEG0022] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His father has asthma. I'm on Metformine, and his dad takes Mizartan for the pressure. Oh, and Luca was on Omprazole as a baby, for the reflux. We stopped it.
[SEG0023] person_4 (PATIENT): Mum. Home.
[SEG0024] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah in a minute, love. The freeway was a car park, took us ages, I'm wrecked.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Metformine and the Mizartan aren't Luca's though, yeah?
[SEG0026] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah, sorry, that's me and his dad. He doesn't take them.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does Luca himself wheeze, or get short of breath?
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): How's his eating and his tummy been?
[SEG0030] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Fine. Eats plenty, no tummy pain.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me look. Dry red patches in both elbow creases and behind both knees, with scratch marks. No crusting, skin's not infected looking. Chest is clear.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): I think this is a flare of eczema. The one percent hydrocortisone isn't quite holding it.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll change the steroid to Advantan ointment, methylprednisolone aceponate nought point one percent. Thin layer once a day on the rough patches for seven days, then stop.

[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep the QV moisturiser, but lay it on thick four times a day, especially a few minutes after a short lukewarm bath. Soap-free wash, and keep his nails short so the scratching does less damage.
[SEG0035] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Do we need to come back, or only if it's worse?
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll book a review in a fortnight. If it starts weeping or he gets a fever, come in sooner rather than waiting.
[SEG0037] person_1 (NURSE): Mm. I can book the fortnight at the desk on your way out.
[SEG0038] person_4 (PATIENT): Go.
